When Phainon was younger, bright-eyed, and curious at the ripe age of eight, she had a best friend. Her best friend was brilliant, too wild and unrestrained for most of the other kids, but somehow as sweet as a kitten to Phainon. He'd share snacks with her at lunch while drawing her cute little cartoons, two inseparable chimaeras going about their daily life, and proudly proclaimed that they represented them. 

Her best friend’s name was Mydeimos, and he was the only boy in the class whom Phainon had ever liked. Like-liked.

The others were too stupid, too boorish, too hung up on the difference in their genders now that they were eight years old and not six or seven, meaning that Phainon was no longer just a playmate to them. No, she was a prospective partner.

She had found it ridiculous. She still did, actually, because there was no reason for eight-year-olds to be walking around on each other’s arms and happily naming themselves ‘boyfriend and girlfriend’ despite not knowing the first thing about being in a relationship.

They didn’t know a thing about shared bank accounts, splitting chores, having arguments over who hogged the blanket, being lectured about how they were hung up on the past and would never find stability in a relationship until they moved on from whoever their heart was stuck on. Normal relationship stuff.

But Mydeimos, or Mydei, as he let Phainon call him, was different.

He never let the fact that Phainon was a girl stop them from playing together; if anything, he made Phainon feel more comfortable, always volunteering himself to be the princess when Phainon wanted to play a knight, or the wife and mother whenever they played house. 

“I like cooking, and babies are cute,” he’d sniff, putting on the costume apron and flipping his single braid, longer than the rest of his hair in its messy cut, behind his shoulder. Phainon liked him so much. “And, you wanna be a lawyer, and you fixed my bike once, so you can be my husband. But you have to make lots of money, otherwise we can’t have loads of kids ‘cause my mama says kids are expensive.”

For Mydei, Phainon would do anything. She wasn’t too fussed about being delegated the traditionally masculine roles — the men in her life were all good role models, and she had always veered towards less girly things, unlike her big sister.

Where Cyrene favoured dresses and dolls and pink, Phainon could always be seen in a scruffy pair of shorts, helping their father do odd jobs around the house. 

It didn't matter that she played Mydei's husband. To Phainon, there was no strict rule for being a girl: some liked dresses, some liked trousers; some liked dolls, some liked cars; some wanted to grow up and start families, some wanted to focus on their careers instead.

It was never something she thought about too much until one day after school, when Mydei had already been picked up by his mother and Phainon was hanging outside the gates as she waited for her father, entertaining herself by eavesdropping on the nearby conversations.

A boy walked past her, holding his elder brother’s hand and listening as the guy spoke like he was imparting great wisdom, “Listen, Aleks, if you want a girlfriend, make sure you go for the quiet ones.”

“Huh?” Aleks was a boy in Phainon's class, a boy too stupid to know the difference in history between the First Flamechase and the Second. Not like Mydei at all. “But, quiet girls are boring.”

Phainon frowned. That was rude. Aleks was acting like he wasn't as entertaining as a seaslug. Mydei hated seaslugs.

Aleks’ brother let out a long-suffering sigh, “Oh, my silly little brother. Let me tell you something important: in life, you're gonna meet a lot of people, and you're gonna have to make yourself stand out. You don't wanna be with a girl who stands out more than you do, otherwise you're not a real man. So, cute girls who don't talk too much and don't try to out-man you — is that a word? Out-man? Whatever — you want to be with those girls.”

“I kinda get it,” Aleks’ voice faded as the pair walked away, but the words had stuck in Phainon's mind.

Guys didn't like girls who stood out. Guys didn't like girls who talked a lot, or who acted more masculine than they were.

To little Phainon, impressionable and curious like a fawn, the first thing that sprang to her mind was the question: did that mean Mydei didn't like her?

Again, in hindsight, as a grown woman looking back on her childhood, Aleks's older brother's words were complete and utter rubbish. Phainon had met plenty of men throughout her life who adored her for the fact that she was a shining star in the legal world, kind and strong, with her hair short and her long legs accentuated by the sharp suit Aglaea had tailored to her figure.

It didn't matter to them that she towered over them even without heels, and curled her lip at their salivating and begging to take her out to dinner. They only cared when she rejected them politely, with a simple, "Sorry, I'm not into guys."

But eight-year-old Phainon took that fateful conversation to heart and vowed to change herself into the ideal girl.

She would probably have to rethink her entire plan for her life, but as long as Mydei stayed with her, she didn't mind too much. Who cared if she would have to hold her tongue in conversation and reduce herself to an accessory for Mydei as he went about his day? It was better than having him wake up one day and realise he didn't like Phainon for being too... too boyish.

As soon as she got home, having been picked up shortly after, Phainon had burst into tears.

"Cy-Cyrene," she had cried, hugging her big sister tight as she was fretted over, "can you teach me to be a girl?"

Cyrene had said something in response, probably trying to discourage her from changing herself to fit such an arbitrary standard of femininity, but it didn't matter.

The next day, Phainon showed up to school in a frilly blue dress, one of Cyrene's hand-me-downs, with a ribbon in her hair and a reserved smile on her face. Most of the class didn't notice, or didn't care, too busy chatting with their friends or practising their times tables.

But Mydei noticed. He always noticed her.

When he met Phainon's eyes across the room, his jaw dropped. Golden eyes widened, and he quickly trotted over with a strange look on his face.

"Why are you dressed like that?" He asked, his brows furrowed cutely as he pinched the fabric of her sleeve.

Phainon's heart sank. "Do you not like it?"

If Mydei didn't like her like this — if he didn't see her as a girl — then how would they ever get married when they were older? Phainon's lip started to quiver. She had only dressed up like this to make him understand that Phainon was willing to change herself for him, to soften her firm edges in an attempt to make him happy, no matter how much she hated it.

For a moment, she stood there, blinking hastily to avoid tears springing to her eyes. But then Mydei took her hand in his and began leading them over to the play area where their friends were already waiting.

"I didn't say that," he muttered, his ears burning pink. "I think you look pretty."

"Really?"

"Yeah. But didn't you say you hate wearing dresses?" Mydei dropped her hand as he reached into the costume basket to take out the briefcase and blazer for Phainon, and the apron for himself. He paused, taking note of the expression on her face. "Why are you smiling like that?"

"I don't hate dresses." She did. Maybe it was only a phase of her childhood, but dresses made her uncomfortable; she didn't like the feeling of the skirt swishing around her legs and flapping whenever she tried to roughhouse with Mydei. She would have preferred to be in a comfortable pair of shorts with a cute top. But she needed to be dainty. "And what's wrong with my smile?"

"It's weird. You normally have your teeth out, like this." His mouth stretched into a broad smile, a radiant thing that displayed a prominent gap from where one of his baby teeth had fallen out, and yet it was far from ordinary for him and only made him look strange. He looked like he was pretending to be someone he wasn't.

"I'm trying to practise being more restrained." Phainon mumbled, and before Mydei had a chance to retort, she quickly cut in, "I want to be the mom today."

Mydei froze. He looked awfully distraught at her words, but he held the apron out to her regardless. "But… I'm always the mom."

"Well, I want a turn." She really didn't, but it was for Mydei's own good. She didn't want him to be made fun of for always pandering to her whims.

None of them enjoyed playing house that day. Phainon tried her best, but her heart just wasn't into playing the mom, and Mydei looked bored out of his mind trying to pretend to be interested in playing Phainon's husband.

Part of Phainon was pleased — this meant that it wasn't just her who felt out of place in their role — but mostly, she felt upset. Was it truly so hard for Mydei to see Phainon as a girl? As a wife? Did he not… like-like her the way she did?

She went home in tears again that day, wailing into her father's arms about how she was doomed to be alone forever because she was too manly to be a girl but too girly to be a boy, and no one would ever love her. Her father, holding back his incredulous chuckles at such severe words from his child, patted her back placatingly and tried to soothe her, but it was fruitless.

It got even worse that same evening, when her parents and sister sat Phainon down on the sofa after dinner, a large tub of ice cream secured in her grasp, to share the devastating news.

"You remember how I applied to that school in Janusopolis, right, Phai?" Cyrene began, tapping her fingers on her knee.

Phainon nodded.

"Well… I got in!" She brandished an acceptance letter in front of Phainon's face, proudly displaying the bold text stating, 'We are delighted to invite Miss Cyrene…' on the creamy paper.

With a cheer, Phainon wrapped her arms around Cyrene in a tight hug. Her sister was brilliant, of course she would be able to get into the school. Cyrene was kind, smart, and sweet; all the adults were always saying she had a bright future ahead of her, no matter what path she chose. A perfect daughter, a perfect sister, a perfect girl. Mydei would probably prefer her. Phainon's smile twitched.

Their father cleared his throat. "We want to support your sister — after all, this school is incredible."

An immediate nod from Phainon. There was no doubt: Cyrene had worked hard and deserved their support.

"But," their mother spoke this time, "honey, that means we'll need to move closer to Janusopolis."

Moving… to Janusopolis? Leaving behind all of their neighbours, their friends, Mydei?

"But—! But…" Phainon wanted to protest, wanted to say something to convince them that they couldn't leave behind this quaint little town with its familiar faces, but then she caught sight of the look on Cyrene's face.

Her smile was shaky, and her eyes were bright with an emotion drifting between fear and resignation. The hand holding tightly onto her acceptance letter was trembling, as though she were fearing that the place she had worked so hard to earn in her dream school would be snatched from her.

Phainon couldn't do that to her big sister.

Her big sister, who always cuddled her close whenever she cried, telling her fantastical stories to distract her from the tribulations of life at eight years old; her sister, who used her pocket money to buy Phainon candies and action figures despite not knowing a single thing about the Chrysos Heirs Cinematic Universe.

Besides, really, what was she leaving behind here? She could always make new friends and form new bonds. Maybe she'd never meet a boy like Mydei again, but… he probably didn't like her like that anyway, so he'd be glad she was gone.

Phainon had made up her mind. Her blue eyes were wide but firm as she resolutely spoke. "Then, we should do it. I don't mind, as long as Cyrene's happy."

Their parents looked surprised at her words, as though they had been expecting a different response. Maybe tears, or whining, or a full-blown tantrum, but Phainon had cried enough for the day, and she wanted to fulfil her sister's wish.

So, it was decided: they'd move over the summer, once the school year had finished, and enrol Phainon in a new school in Janusopolis, where she'd start afresh. Cyrene would go to her academy, their father would request a transfer for his job, and their mother would take up work under a branch of their godmother's clothing company.

And Mydei would be left behind, along with Phainon's tears and her childhood puppy-crush.
